analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil company stock buybacks at 10% to fund clean energy and home-heating aid for low-income households.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2008 with no cosponsors, referred to four House committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would place a 10% tax on every stock buyback executed by a major integrated oil company — when the company repurchases its own shares. The money would go into a federal Clean Energy Fund, with 60% set aside for renewable energy, energy efficiency, and related research, and 40% sent to the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance program, which helps poor households pay heating and cooling bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that rely on federal energy assistance to heat and cool their homes, plus clean-energy industries and anyone who benefits from expanded renewables, efficiency programs, and energy research funded by the new trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households and clean energy programs

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates 40% of the fund to the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance program, which pays heating and cooling bills for poor households [S2][S3].

Appropriates 60% of the fund to offset legislation accelerating domestic renewable energy and alternative fuels, promoting energy efficiency and conservation, and increasing research and deployment of clean energy technologies [S2][S3].
The money comes from a 10% excise tax on stock repurchases by major integrated oil companies, so the funding burden falls on a single profitable industry rather than general taxpayers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies, which would owe a 10% tax on the market value of every share they buy back, reducing cash available for buybacks and shareholder returns.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major integrated oil companies doing buybacks

drawbacks.text: The bill is a funding shell: 60% of the fund is reserved only to 'offset the cost of subsequent legislation,' so the actual clean-energy spending would still require Congress to pass separate bills later [S3].
A tax aimed narrowly at oil company buybacks gives companies an easy path to avoid it by shifting cash returns to dividends instead of repurchases, weakening the revenue base the fund depends on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The household energy aid is real and immediate, and taxing oil company buybacks concentrates the cost on a highly profitable industry rather than ordinary taxpayers. But the bill is partly aspirational: the majority of the money only becomes available if future legislation claims it, and companies could restructure buybacks into dividends to shrink the revenue. It is a targeted, modest-sized proposal rather than a comprehensive energy policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2008 and referred to four House committees, one of which sent it to a subcommittee, and it never moved again before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on May 22, 2008 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Science and Technology, and Education and Labor committees [S5].
On June 3, 2008, it was referred to the Energy and Environment subcommittee [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no vote was held in either chamber, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies, which keep their stock buybacks untaxed, and no one else in particular — low-income households never saw the heating aid. Because the bill drew no cosponsors and no committee action, its failure reflects an absence of legislative momentum as much as organized opposition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies, which kept buybacks untaxed

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the tax provision (first referral)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill, no other members of either party signed on, and the Republican-led chambers of 2008 took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill puts a 10% tax on their stock buybacks, directly reducing cash returned to shareholders. Oil companies have historically opposed such targeted levies, and their interest here runs against the bill's energy-assistance and clean-energy spending.

60% of the fund would offset spending on renewables, alternative fuels, efficiency, and clean-energy research, creating demand and investment for these industries. Their gain tracks with the public interest in cheaper, cleaner energy.

industries.industry: Low-income energy assistance program (LIHEAP) providers and recipients
industries.note: 40% of the fund is a dedicated revenue stream for LIHEAP, which helps low-income households pay utility bills.
